Speaker: D:
Text: Alright, we’re recording.

Speaker: D:
Text: So, my name is Kendriana Drayton and I am here with Ms. Emily Williams.

Speaker: D:
Text: I’m a part of the oral history program at the University of Florida with the African American History Project.

Speaker: D:
Text: Will you introduce us to you please?

Speaker: D:
Text: Give us your name.

Speaker: W:
Text: My name is Ms. Emily J Williams.

Speaker: D:
Text: J stands for?

Speaker: W:
Text: Jones.

Speaker: D:
Text: How did you get your name?

Speaker: W:
Text: My mother and grandmother’s name.

Speaker: D:
Text: Okay.

Speaker: D:
Text: When and where were you born?

Speaker: W:
Text: I was born 1946 in Hastings, Florida.

Speaker: D:
Text: Were you born to a midwife or a hospital?

Speaker: W:
Text: A midwife.

Speaker: D:
Text: Okay, who are your parents?

Speaker: W:
Text: Mr. and Mrs. Walter McCormick.

Speaker: D:
Text: You know where they were born?

Speaker: W:
Text: In Georgia.

Speaker: D:
Text: You know what they did for a living?

Speaker: W:
Text: Farm labor.

Speaker: D:
Text: Okay.

Speaker: D:
Text: Who were your siblings?

Speaker: W:
Text: Question?

Speaker: D:
Text: Your siblings.

Speaker: W:
Text: What about my siblings, right?

Speaker: D:
Text: Unh-uh.

Speaker: D:
Text: Who your brothers and sisters, your brothers and sisters.

Speaker: W:
Text: Who are they, what they names?

Speaker: W:
Text: My oldest sister’s name is Clarissa, Ulla, Carrie, Linda, and Deborah.

Speaker: D:
Text: Okay.

Speaker: D:
Text: Can you give me the address of your home where you all grew up?

Speaker: W:
Text: We moved different places.

Speaker: D:
Text: Okay.

Speaker: D:
Text: Around Hastings?

Speaker: W:
Text: Yeah we lived at East Hastings first, and then we moved to the address on Walt McCormick road near the county line.

Speaker: D:
Text: Okay.

Speaker: W:
Text: Of Putnam and St. Johns County.

Speaker: D:
Text: So right in between St. Augustine and Palatka?

Speaker: W:
Text: Uh-huh.

Speaker: W:
Text: It’s on that — it’s mostly like what’s on that county line, lived on the county line by Putnam and St. Johns County.

Speaker: D:
Text: Okay.

Speaker: D:
Text: Did you see a lot of officials traveling?

Speaker: D:
Text: Living between St. Augustine and Palatka?

Speaker: W:
Text: Yes.

Speaker: D:
Text: What about trains?

Speaker: W:
Text: Yes.

Speaker: W:
Text: There was a train.

Speaker: W:
Text: A railroad track and the train came through where we lived.

Speaker: D:
Text: Did you all go to the station often?

Speaker: W:
Text: It was in town, Hastings, the station is located in town.

Speaker: W:
Text: In the city of Hastings .

Speaker: D:
Text: Did you ever go on the train?

Speaker: D:
Text: Did you all ever?

Speaker: W:
Text: No, no.

Speaker: D:
Text: So what kind of chores did you have to do growing up?

Speaker: D:
Text: How did you divide it amongst your sisters?

Speaker: W:
Text: We did field labor, house cleaning, that’s it .

Speaker: W:
Text: Whatever our hands find to do, that’s what we did.

Speaker: D:
Text: So who did most of the cooking?

Speaker: W:
Text: Our mom.

Speaker: D:
Text: What kind of foods did you eat?

Speaker: W:
Text: Different kinds.

Speaker: W:
Text: Whatever she cooked, that’s what we ate.

Speaker: D:
Text: And that was from your own garden?

Speaker: W:
Text: It always had the vegetables in there, at the back of the house.

Speaker: W:
Text: We had a field with all different types of vegetables.

Speaker: D:
Text: Okay.

Speaker: D:
Text: Was there a separate shopping store for Black people in Hastings?

Speaker: W:
Text: Several stores in Hastings, grocery stores, and shopping stores.

Speaker: D:
Text: That was segregated?

Speaker: W:
Text: Yes.

Speaker: D:
Text: How was shopping?

Speaker: D:
Text: What was a normal shopping trip like?

Speaker: W:
Text: It was nice.

Speaker: W:
Text: I enjoyed it.

Speaker: W:
Text: I went a lot with my grandmother.

Speaker: W:
Text: She took me with her a lot to the grocery stores.

Speaker: D:
Text: You know the name of the store?

Speaker: W:
Text: Levitt’s.

Speaker: W:
Text: That’s the grocery store, and the dressing store was the Five and Ten Cents store.

Speaker: W:
Text: And they had another store, Miss Carly’s store, and next door they called the Five and Ten Cents store.

Speaker: D:
Text: What was sold there?

Speaker: W:
Text: Well so, they packed every little thing in there, like for houseware and stuff like that.

Speaker: D:
Text: Okay.

Speaker: D:
Text: What was it like going downtown?

Speaker: D:
Text: Was it kinda busy or was it kinda slow?

Speaker: W:
Text: Well, different seasons.

Speaker: W:
Text: When it was harvesting time for potatoes, it was very busy, and cabbage season was very busy.

Speaker: D:
Text: So you saw a lot of people come into town for that?

Speaker: W:
Text: Yes. Uh-huh.

Speaker: D:
Text: Okay.

Speaker: D:
Text: So you say you went a lot of times to the store with your grandmother?

Speaker: D:
Text: What was her name?

Speaker: W:
Text: Her name was Emily.

Speaker: W:
Text: Emily Dean.

Speaker: D:
Text: So did your dad, Walter Mc Cormick , did he do a lot more of the selling and growing of the food?

Speaker: W:
Text: He had his own produce.

Speaker: W:
Text: And there were other stores that sold other produce, places to buy produce also.

Speaker: D:
Text: So he had like a stand or a store?

Speaker: W:
Text: No, he had it at the house.

Speaker: W:
Text: And he would just like raise it in and just like, give it away.

Speaker: W:
Text: He didn’t never sell it, he would just raise it and give it away.

Speaker: D:
Text: So people kinda looked for him to do the good thing?

Speaker: D:
Text: Good deed?

Speaker: W:
Text: Uh-huh.

Speaker: W:
Text: That’s what he did.

Speaker: D:
Text: Was there ever any type of intimidation from the White community?

Speaker: D:
Text: With him being so nice and helping the Blacks?

Speaker: W:
Text: Everybody mostly got ten along together.

Speaker: W:
Text: This community thing is just nice.

Speaker: W:
Text: Everyone did what they’re supposed to do.

Speaker: W:
Text: Tend to their own business.

Speaker: D:
Text: Okay.

Speaker: D:
Text: So about how old were you when you kinda realized you were Black?

Speaker: W:
Text: I was about one.

Speaker: D:
Text: Really?

Speaker: W:
Text: Uh-huh.

Speaker: D:
Text: What did it mean?

Speaker: W:
Text: Hm?

Speaker: D:
Text: What did it mean?

Speaker: W:
Text: What did it mean?

Speaker: D:
Text: Uh-huh.

Speaker: W:
Text: I was just happy, I was always a happy little girl.

Speaker: D:
Text: Okay, so you were aware of being Black, but were you aware of racism?

Speaker: D:
Text: Did it kinda make you nervous or anything?

Speaker: W:
Text: Not really.

Speaker: W:
Text: I just loved to communicate and help with people.

Speaker: W:
Text: The way I am now.

Speaker: W:
Text: I was like that from a little girl.

Speaker: D:
Text: Just talk and approach people and just?

Speaker: W:
Text: Yes.

Speaker: D:
Text: Okay.

Speaker: D:
Text: So segregation as a child wasn’t really too hard.

Speaker: D:
Text: It just was —

Speaker: W:
Text: It was just, just normal.

Speaker: W:
Text: Because I just loved to talk.

Speaker: W:
Text: See people and talk with them.

Speaker: D:
Text: You didn’t let it be a barrier.

Speaker: W:
Text: No.

Speaker: D:
Text: So where did you all play?

Speaker: D:
Text: What kind of things did you all do growing up in the neighborhood?

Speaker: W:
Text: We played games.

Speaker: D:
Text: Was it a very close neighborhood or was it kinda spread out?

Speaker: W:
Text: It was kind of knitted, you know.

Speaker: W:
Text: Because we all had to go to school together, and all that.

Speaker: W:
Text: So it’s nice.

Speaker: D:
Text: Okay and what school did you go to?

Speaker: W:
Text: Walter E. Harris high school.

Speaker: D:
Text: How did you get to school every day?

Speaker: W:
Text: Bus.

Speaker: D:
Text: On bus?

Speaker: W:
Text: Um-hm, school bus.

Speaker: D:
Text: What kinda route did you take?

Speaker: W:
Text: All through the woods and everywhere they had to pick the kids up.

Speaker: W:
Text: It was all into the woods to pick the kids up.

Speaker: D:
Text: Was it a long bus ride?

Speaker: W:
Text: Yes, it was pretty long because we had to go all the way into the woods to get the kids to get them to school.

Speaker: D:
Text: So then were some kids from St. Augustine, or was it mostly people coming from—

Speaker: W:
Text: It was Black.

Speaker: W:
Text: It was most the people in the surrounding area of Hastings.

Speaker: D:
Text: Would that be like Spuds and?

Speaker: W:
Text: Yes.

Speaker: D:
Text: Okay.

Speaker: D:
Text: So who were some of your teachers?

Speaker: W:
Text: Ms. Rosa Hawkins, Ms. Lucy Carver, Ms. Aretha Mary, Mr. Lawrence, Mr. James Campbell, Mr. Coach Henderson.

Speaker: D:
Text: Were they all Black?

Speaker: W:
Text: Ms. Cory Harrison .

Speaker: W:
Text: Yes, they were all Black.

Speaker: D:
Text: Okay.

Speaker: D:
Text: Did you go there for all twelve years?

Speaker: W:
Text: Yes, I attended.

Speaker: D:
Text: What kind of—

Speaker: W:
Text: Yes.

Speaker: D:
Text: About how long was your school year?

Speaker: D:
Text: How long were you in school?

Speaker: W:
Text: First through twelfth grade.

Speaker: D:
Text: What role did school play in your community?

Speaker: W:
Text: Played a great deal, because back then teachers believed in you learning.

Speaker: W:
Text: You had to learn.

Speaker: W:
Text: You didn’t go to school every day just to sit around and play.

Speaker: W:
Text: You went to school to learn.

Speaker: W:
Text: To actually talk to.

Speaker: D:
Text: When you say learn, it sounds like you’re talking about more than just reading and writing.

Speaker: W:
Text: Right.

Speaker: W:
Text: You had like home making and you had like, they had the gathering of the vegetables.

Speaker: W:
Text: You had to clean those and get them prepared to go into the freezer.

Speaker: W:
Text: Yeah, we did all —

Speaker: D:
Text: The home, like, preparing and organizing things and—

Speaker: W:
Text: Right.

Speaker: D:
Text: Did you use some of those skills when you started to work?

Speaker: W:
Text: Oh sure.

Speaker: W:
Text: I already knew how to cook.

Speaker: W:
Text: My mom and dad had already taught us how to work .

Speaker: W:
Text: And we already knew what to do.

Speaker: W:
Text: Uh- huh.

Speaker: W:
Text: It didn’t come hard, you already knew what to do.

Speaker: D:
Text: So, you kind of felt like that that was what’s expected of you, like I already know how to do these things?

Speaker: W:
Text: Yes.

Speaker: W:
Text: We did whatever it took to get the job done.

Speaker: D:
Text: So what were some of your first jobs?

Speaker: W:
Text: Cleaning house, cooking, making your bed, raking yards, cutting wood.

Speaker: W:
Text: We did all of that.

Speaker: D:
Text: You cut wood?

Speaker: W:
Text: Yes, with the axe, for the heater.

Speaker: W:
Text: You had to have wood to go into the heater.

Speaker: W:
Text: You had to pump your water with the pump.

Speaker: W:
Text: Pump water.

Speaker: W:
Text: Yes.

Speaker: W:
Text: You had to do all of that.

Speaker: D:
Text: And about how much did you get paid?

Speaker: W:
Text: No, you didn’t really get paid, that was your daily house chore jobs.

Speaker: D:
Text: Oh, for your house.

Speaker: W:
Text: Yes!

Speaker: W:
Text: At home!

Speaker: W:
Text: You got to do all of that!

Speaker: W:
Text: You know?

Speaker: W:
Text: At home!

Speaker: W:
Text: Yes!

Speaker: D:
Text: Before you even went out to work.

Speaker: W:
Text: Yes!

Speaker: W:
Text: Yes!

Speaker: W:
Text: Well we did field labor too, but these was regular around the house.

Speaker: W:
Text: You had to do all of that at home.

Speaker: D:
Text: You had to do homework.

Speaker: W:
Text: Yes!

Speaker: W:
Text: Everyday!

Speaker: W:
Text: That wasn’t a one- time thing, that was a everyday thing.

Speaker: D:
Text: So what would you do to take a break?

Speaker: D:
Text: How would you kind of relax?

Speaker: W:
Text: Oh, you would rest a little bit, but you go right back to the job.

Speaker: W:
Text: Right back to the grinding pole, ‘cause Rosa didn’t play, my mom didn’t play the radio with you.

Speaker: D:
Text: So she was very stern and making sure you did your work?

Speaker: W:
Text: Yes, yes.

Speaker: W:
Text: She believed in you learning.

Speaker: D:
Text: Even outside of school?

Speaker: W:
Text: She always said, “You gonna know how to do more than one thing.”

Speaker: W:
Text: And you could rest assured you’d learn how to do more than one thing.

Speaker: D:
Text: So they settled here in Hastings?

Speaker: W:
Text: Yes.

Speaker: D:
Text: Do you know where she went to school?

Speaker: W:
Text: They used to live in Daytona.

Speaker: W:
Text: They went to school in Daytona Beach.

Speaker: D:
Text: Okay.

Speaker: D:
Text: So you said that she liked for you all to do more than one thing.

Speaker: W:
Text: Yeah, she said, “Y’all are going to know how to do more than just one thing.”

Speaker: D:
Text: So she was a teacher?

Speaker: W:
Text: Yes.

Speaker: W:
Text: And she taught us how to do all types of jobs.

Speaker: D:
Text: What about church?

Speaker: W:
Text: Oh yes, you attended church too.

Speaker: W:
Text: Sunday school.

Speaker: W:
Text: Every Sunday.

Speaker: W:
Text: And she would make sure that she would feed you before you leave.

Speaker: W:
Text: She would get up every Sunday morning.

Speaker: W:
Text: She would prepare baked biscuits, fried chicken, cooked grits, and eggs.

Speaker: W:
Text: And made lemonade.

Speaker: W:
Text: And that would be your breakfast before you were off to Sunday school and church.

Speaker: W:
Text: On Sunday mornings.

Speaker: D:
Text: Lemonade.

Speaker: W:
Text: Yes, lemonade.

Speaker: D:
Text: But so, through the week, she did what for a living?

Speaker: W:
Text: Worked in the fields.

Speaker: W:
Text: Cooking, ironing, washing clothes.

Speaker: D:
Text: Did they own any of the land?

Speaker: W:
Text: We owned our house.

Speaker: W:
Text: We rented first and then later on, they had John Walter to build a home across the street from where we were renting, and then we moved into our house.

Speaker: D:
Text: About how old were you then?

Speaker: W:
Text: I would say about eight.

Speaker: D:
Text: Okay, so what was the holidays like?

Speaker: D:
Text: Would everyone kinda go there, or would they go to grandma

Speaker: D:
Text: Emily’s house?

Speaker: W:
Text: Well it was just at home.

Speaker: W:
Text: Playing with our toys.

Speaker: W:
Text: Sitting around after we cooked we sit around and eat and talk.

Speaker: W:
Text: Just spend that Christmas together.

Speaker: W:
Text: Open our Christmas gifts.

Speaker: D:
Text: Did you all take any family photos?

Speaker: W:
Text: No we didn’t take — unh-uh.

Speaker: D:
Text: Were there any type of clubs or social things in Hastings?

Speaker: D:
Text: Like a movie theater?

Speaker: W:
Text: No, we had TV’s, and go to watch movies .

Speaker: W:
Text: We had to stay at home and watch TV.

Speaker: D:
Text: Was there a reason why?

Speaker: W:
Text: She just said that we just had to stay home and watch the black and white TV.

Speaker: W:
Text: She’d never let us go to movies.

Speaker: W:
Text: And really if you went, you would have to travel to St. Augustine or Palatka.

Speaker: W:
Text: So they would never allow us to go there.

Speaker: D:
Text: How did they find Hastings?

Speaker: W:
Text: I don’t really know how they really found that place.

Speaker: W:
Text: They just decided that they came, and I guessed they loved it, and

Speaker: W:
Text: that’s where they settled at.

Speaker: D:
Text: So I know it’s near St. Augustine.

Speaker: D:
Text: Do you remember Martin Luther King or any civil rights figures come into St. Augustine in the 60s?

Speaker: W:
Text: Yes. Uh-huh.

Speaker: D:
Text: Can you tell me about them?

Speaker: W:
Text: Oh it was at Brighton, over there, because they were saying that the Ku Klux Klans and all of those was over there in St. Augustine, and they were fighting and all that when Martin Luther King and Andrew Jackson and them came to St. Augustine.

Speaker: W:
Text: And it was just, it was like scary to hear them talk about what was happening over there.

Speaker: D:
Text: And so you were in Hastings?

Speaker: W:
Text: Uh-huh, in school.

Speaker: D:
Text: So grade school?

Speaker: W:
Text: I was in school.

Speaker: W:
Text: Uh -huh.

Speaker: W:
Text: I was in school then.

Speaker: W:
Text: During that time.

Speaker: D:
Text: They didn’t want to or think about doing any protesting?

Speaker: W:
Text: Some of them in St. Augustine, we heard it that they were doing it, but not in Hastings.

Speaker: W:
Text: Unh-uh.

Speaker: W:
Text: They didn’t have any of that over in Hastings.

Speaker: D:
Text: Kinda just kept things quiet.

Speaker: W:
Text: Yes, uh-huh.

Speaker: D:
Text: Did you feel safer that way?

Speaker: W:
Text: It was kinda frightening to hear about that.

Speaker: W:
Text: Was it being near or close to where we live, it was just kind of frightening.

Speaker: D:
Text: When did you kind of first become aware of segregation?

Speaker: D:
Text: Like in grade school?

Speaker: W:
Text: During the time when we were in school, grade school, we were hearing about what was happening in St. Augustine.

Speaker: D:
Text: Do you remember any personal experiences of racism?

Speaker: W:
Text: Not really.

Speaker: D:
Text: Do you remember any formal ways people fought racism?

Speaker: D:
Text: Like how Black people took a stand against racism?

Speaker: W:
Text: You would just like, hear about that.

Speaker: W:
Text: You know about what happening over there in St. Augustine.

Speaker: W:
Text: People were protesting, and talked about a lot of different things that really wasn’t right towards Black people.

Speaker: D:
Text: How’d it make you feel?

Speaker: W:
Text: It made me feel kinda bad about it.

Speaker: D:
Text: What helped?

Speaker: D:
Text: Did anything help?

Speaker: W:
Text: Yeah, but you know when you talk about things, it makes you feel better when you can bring it out and talk about it, it makes you feel better.

Speaker: D:
Text: You didn’t do this through a counselor, you kinda just did it with close—

Speaker: W:
Text: Right, uh-huh, friends and stuff like that.

Speaker: D:
Text: After you graduated from Walter E. Harris, how was your college application process?

Speaker: D:
Text: How did you —

Speaker: W:
Text: It went very good.

Speaker: W:
Text: It went good.

Speaker: D:
Text: Where did you apply to?

Speaker: W:
Text: Collier-Blocker Junior College.

Speaker: D:
Text: Okay, and why that college?

Speaker: W:
Text: Well I just wanted to go.

Speaker: W:
Text: I thought it was a good idea and everything, and I wanted to try and go.

Speaker: W:
Text: So I did go.

Speaker: D:
Text: Any of your other siblings went to college?

Speaker: W:
Text: No, I think one.

Speaker: D:
Text: Okay, what was your experience like at Collier?

Speaker: W:
Text: It was a great experience.

Speaker: W:
Text: I enjoyed classes, and being with the other kids and talking and discussing our classes, and I had a job working in the library.

Speaker: W:
Text: And I enjoyed it, going there after classes.

Speaker: W:
Text: I would go into the library and work in the library, do typing, and filing books in the library.

Speaker: W:
Text: And that was my job, and I got paid to do that.

Speaker: D:
Text: About how much?

Speaker: W:
Text: Wow.

Speaker: W:
Text: It wasn’t very much, but it helped.

Speaker: W:
Text: Maybe around, about, I would guess about three or four dollars an hour, something like that.

Speaker: D:
Text: Were you still living at home?

Speaker: W:
Text: Yes.

Speaker: D:
Text: Okay.

Speaker: D:
Text: So how did you get to Collier-Blocker?

Speaker: W:
Text: Bus.

Speaker: D:
Text: Where was Collier-Blocker?

Speaker: W:
Text: Located in Palatka.

Speaker: D:
Text: Okay, so it was about how long of a bus ride every day?

Speaker: W:
Text: It wasn’t too long.

Speaker: W:
Text: Let’s say I would catch that bus off of two zero seven.

Speaker: W:
Text: It would go into Palatka and drop the kids off because they had a bus that would run from St. Augustine to Palatka, and from Palatka back to St. Augustine, picking up students that attended Collier -Blocker.

Speaker: D:
Text: So that was a Black college?

Speaker: D:
Text: A predominantly Black college?

Speaker: W:
Text: Yes, uh-huh.

Speaker: D:
Text: And so was your high school?

Speaker: W:
Text: Yes.

Speaker: D:
Text: Was it integrated?

Speaker: W:
Text: No.

Speaker: D:
Text: Okay.

Speaker: D:
Text: Were you one of the first in your family to go to college?

Speaker: D:
Text: Did your mom, or grandma, or grandad go?

Speaker: W:
Text: No. No.

Speaker: D:
Text: Did they ever talk about school?

Speaker: D:
Text: College?

Speaker: W:
Text: No, because they said they had to start working.

Speaker: W:
Text: They had to stop going to school and go to work in the fields.

Speaker: W:
Text: So they were out and about in the field for sixth or seventh grade.

Speaker: D:
Text: Did they know how to read?

Speaker: W:
Text: My grandmother, she read a bit and I took up time with her and read a lot with her and stuff like that.

Speaker: W:
Text: I took up time.

Speaker: W:
Text: She really wanted me to read to her and I would read to her, yes.

Speaker: D:
Text: Do you remember her birth date?

Speaker: W:
Text: I believe they say her birthday was Dec ember the twenty-forth.

Speaker: D:
Text: Okay.

Speaker: W:
Text: Uh-huh, I remember them saying that her birthday was Christmas Eve.

Speaker: D:
Text: So they kinda had to stop going to school to work?

Speaker: W:
Text: Yes, because they had to work in the fields.

Speaker: D:
Text: With their different families.

Speaker: W:
Text: Right.

Speaker: D:
Text: Okay, did you hear them talk about slavery, anyone?

Speaker: D:
Text: Grandma, granddad?

Speaker: W:
Text: They just always talked about how they had always worked.

Speaker: W:
Text: Worked hard.

Speaker: D:
Text: What kind of work did they do?

Speaker: W:
Text: Field labor.

Speaker: D:
Text: Okay, what do you remember about segregation in the 90s — I mean, sorry — the 1970s?

Speaker: D:
Text: You were graduated out of school.

Speaker: D:
Text: So did you notice it more in the community, or did you hear about maybe your younger sisters having to go to an integrated high school, or college, or anything?

Speaker: W:
Text: Not really, I just really found that out when after I married and moved here, and how the school was.

Speaker: W:
Text: They had the Black school, the White school, and then they integrated some from this school, and it would take them up town to the White school.

Speaker: D:
Text: What was the name of that school?

Speaker: W:
Text: Miller Intermediate School.

Speaker: D:
Text: That was in St. Augustine?

Speaker: W:
Text: No that was here, in Crescent City.

Speaker: D:
Text: Oh Miller Intermediate was here?

Speaker: W:
Text: Uh-huh, yes.

Speaker: W:
Text: It was here, in Crescent City.

Speaker: D:
Text: What was that like?

Speaker: D:
Text: Was that something that you all talked about?

Speaker: W:
Text: Well I used to like see the kids when the buses — half the kids on the bus I just would see that.

Speaker: W:
Text: Since I was living here in the 60s.

Speaker: D:
Text: How was the climate here in Crescent City?

Speaker: D:
Text: Was it different than Hastings?

Speaker: W:
Text: It was about the same.

Speaker: D:
Text: So there was like Black shops here, a Black community here?

Speaker: W:
Text: Yeah, they have this —they still had the school separated, the Blacks out here and the Whites was uptown.

Speaker: W:
Text: And that’s how they had it.

Speaker: D:
Text: When did you first vote?

Speaker: W:
Text: When I turned eighteen.

Speaker: D:
Text: Do you remember who was running, on the ballot?

Speaker: W:
Text: I don’t remember who was actually running then, but I voted.

Speaker: W:
Text: I had already registered to vote

Speaker: D:
Text: Was that experience challenging or was it pretty easy?

Speaker: W:
Text: It was okay.

Speaker: W:
Text: It was okay.

Speaker: D:
Text: Okay.

Speaker: D:
Text: Did your parents talk about voting, or the importance of voting?

Speaker: W:
Text: Yeah, they talked about it.

Speaker: W:
Text: Saying how important that it was to vote.

Speaker: D:
Text: Did they hold any high positions in the community?

Speaker: W:
Text: Not really, they just was like church parent people, and Christian people, and they always tried to help save out people in the community.

Speaker: W:
Text: Mom would cook and dad would go and get the people, and bring them to the house and feed them.

Speaker: W:
Text: They were really communicative workers and helpers that helped people that were in need.

Speaker: W:
Text: Yes, they did that.

Speaker: D:
Text: You want to get the water?

Speaker: D:
Text: I think I asked you if anyone else had been to college before you, right?

Speaker: W:
Text: Right, no.

Speaker: D:
Text: But did your mom, or grandma, or dad, or grandparent want you to go to college?

Speaker: W:
Text: Yes, uh-huh.

Speaker: D:
Text: How did they support you?

Speaker: W:
Text: They gave me money.

Speaker: D:
Text: Okay, did you have to pay per class or?

Speaker: W:
Text: Not really, no.

Speaker: W:
Text: I didn’t have to pay.

Speaker: D:
Text: So college was pretty inexpensive?

Speaker: W:
Text: Yes, back then it was pretty much inexpensive.

Speaker: W:
Text: They really needed the students, because they did have farms and they wanted the students to come so that they could use the farms that they had gotten.

Speaker: W:
Text: For kids to attend college.

Speaker: D:
Text: So you went to college, and what did you study?

Speaker: W:
Text: Business administration.

Speaker: D:
Text: Around what year was this?

Speaker: W:
Text: It was in the year of 1964 and 65.

Speaker: D:
Text: So you went for two years?

Speaker: W:
Text: Um-hm.

Speaker: W:
Text: A year and a half, something like that.

Speaker: D:
Text: And then you moved here, to Crescent City?

Speaker: W:
Text: Yes.

Speaker: D:
Text: How was that transition?

Speaker: W:
Text: It was nice.

Speaker: D:
Text: Were you able to continue going to school once you moved here?

Speaker: W:
Text: No I didn’t go after I had moved here, down here, I stopped going.

Speaker: D:
Text: What did you do?

Speaker: W:
Text: I started working.

Speaker: W:
Text: Had gotten a job and started working.

Speaker: D:
Text: What kinda work was available?

Speaker: W:
Text: Like cutting fern.

Speaker: D:
Text: In the 60s?

Speaker: W:
Text: Uh-huh, yes.

Speaker: D:
Text: And did you get paid a little bit more cutting fern than working at the library, or was it a different time?

Speaker: W:
Text: It was a little more.

Speaker: W:
Text: I earned more money.

Speaker: D:
Text: Okay, so was it the same chore list, of house things to be done once you kind of got a house of your own?

Speaker: W:
Text: Yes, uh-huh.

Speaker: D:
Text: Still had a lot of work to do?

Speaker: W:
Text: Yes.

Speaker: D:
Text: How did you kind of incorporate family with work?

Speaker: W:
Text: It worked out pretty good cause I had to get a babysitter, keep someone to watch my kids after I had them.

Speaker: D:
Text: Did you have talks with any of your children about the Black history of segregation and how schools were integrated before they started school?

Speaker: W:
Text: Not too much.

Speaker: W:
Text: Wasn’t really a big problem.

Speaker: D:
Text: Wasn’t a big problem.

Speaker: W:
Text: No, wasn’t really a big problem with that.

Speaker: D:
Text: Did you talk to them just about being Black in America?

Speaker: W:
Text: Yes.

Speaker: D:
Text: What kind of things?

Speaker: W:
Text: Just to go and get more education than what I’ve got, I always instilled that in them.

Speaker: D:
Text: It was for better opportunities, or —

Speaker: W:
Text: Yes, uh-huh, that and jobs.

Speaker: W:
Text: Stuff like that.

Speaker: D:
Text: While you were in college, did you visit or interact any White colleges or White students?

Speaker: W:
Text: Not really, unh-uh.

Speaker: D:
Text: Did you want to?

Speaker: W:
Text: It didn’t really matter.

Speaker: W:
Text: Make no big deal out of that.

Speaker: D:
Text: Were you close with some of the Black professors you had in college?

Speaker: D:
Text: Or did they know your family or anything?

Speaker: W:
Text: Not really, unh-uh, no.

Speaker: D:
Text: Did you ever travel to FAMU’s homecoming or?

Speaker: W:
Text: No.

Speaker: D:
Text: Okay.

Speaker: D:
Text: Well, since integration, do you feel like the community has gotten better?

Speaker: D:
Text: Do you think there’s been progress made since the 60s?

Speaker: W:
Text: There’s progress, some, but it’s a lot of more work to get done.

Speaker: D:
Text: What do you hope kids in the future can do?

Speaker: D:
Text: Or families could do?

Speaker: W:
Text: Work more.

Speaker: W:
Text: You know, closely together.

Speaker: W:
Text: To improve things.

Speaker: W:
Text: There really are, or has been— there’s always room for improvement.

Speaker: D:
Text: I guess the takeaway, you always want people to know what about you?

Speaker: W:
Text: To know about me?

Speaker: D:
Text: Uh-huh, like your life motto or things that’s kinda helped you get —

Speaker: W:
Text: Yes, ‘cause I love to talk to them a lot and discuss things, you know, which I enjoy talking with people and being involved.

Speaker: W:
Text: I enjoy that.

Speaker: D:
Text: What got you in the spirit of giving?

Speaker: W:
Text: My parents.

Speaker: W:
Text: They always taught us.

Speaker: W:
Text: It’s a generational thing, it’s from one generation to the other, and that’s the way we were raised, that way.

Speaker: D:
Text: Did you all go to the beach?

Speaker: W:
Text: Yeah, it was like the special occasion like, Easter, something like that.

Speaker: W:
Text: Easter, I can remember that.

Speaker: D:
Text: To St. Augustine?

Speaker: W:
Text: Yes, to Crescent Beach.

Speaker: D:
Text: Crescent Beach?

Speaker: W:
Text: Yes, Easter.

Speaker: D:
Text: How old were you?

Speaker: W:
Text: Just around about seven or eight, something like that.

Speaker: W:
Text: I can remember that.

Speaker: W:
Text: Dad and mom used to always love to take us to the beach for Easter.

Speaker: D:
Text: I like that.

Speaker: W:
Text: Yes, Sunday evening.

Speaker: D:
Text: So when did you kind of realize that you were gonna grow up and I guess have a family?

Speaker: W:
Text: As I turned like eighteen, going on nineteen, something like that.

Speaker: D:
Text: And did you have, or, how many children?

Speaker: W:
Text: Five.

Speaker: D:
Text: Five.

Speaker: W:
Text: Five kids.

Speaker: W:
Text: Uh-huh.

Speaker: D:
Text: Were they all delivered by midwifes?

Speaker: W:
Text: No, not all of them.

Speaker: D:
Text: Okay.

Speaker: W:
Text: There was three, let me see, one.

Speaker: W:
Text: No, I had two that they were in the hospital — three delivered in the hospital, and two delivered by midwifes.

Speaker: W:
Text: That’s what I had.

Speaker: D:
Text: Do you feel like technology has gotten different or gotten better?

Speaker: W:
Text: It’s better.

Speaker: D:
Text: Do you find it easy to use?

Speaker: W:
Text: Yes, it is.

Speaker: D:
Text: Okay.

Speaker: D:
Text: So you did a lot of family work here, and you said you were married when you moved here?

Speaker: D:
Text: To Crescent City?

Speaker: W:
Text: I got married and moved to Crescent City.

Speaker: D:
Text: Okay.

Speaker: D:
Text: How was the courting process?

Speaker: W:
Text: It was nice.

Speaker: W:
Text: It was okay.

Speaker: D:
Text: Did he ask for your hand in marriage?

Speaker: W:
Text: Uh-huh.

Speaker: W:
Text: Yes!

Speaker: D:
Text: To your parents?

Speaker: W:
Text: Yes!

Speaker: D:
Text: Oh that was the custom?

Speaker: W:
Text: Yes!

Speaker: D:
Text: Okay.

Speaker: D:
Text: Okay.

Speaker: D:
Text: I feel like marriage customs, maybe they changed or not.

Speaker: D:
Text: I think my mom said it was in the — you all announced it in the newspaper?

Speaker: W:
Text: I don’t know, it might’ve been, I don’t know, it’s been so long.

Speaker: W:
Text: Don’t know about that.

Speaker: D:
Text: Okay.

Speaker: D:
Text: Can you tell me about this, moving here, and how did you all go about meeting neighbors and talking to other people?

Speaker: W:
Text: It was nice.

Speaker: W:
Text: I went out and met people, people in the neighborhood, and talked.

Speaker: W:
Text: Walked around, it was nice.

Speaker: D:
Text: Oh, so just kinda like door to door?

Speaker: W:
Text: Yeah, that’s how it went, yeah, um -hm.

Speaker: D:
Text: Do you feel like people do those things anymore?

Speaker: W:
Text: I don’t really know whether they still do that now or not.

Speaker: W:
Text: I don’t know, people are so busy now.

Speaker: W:
Text: Whatever they have to do, they have to hurry and all of this, so.

Speaker: D:
Text: But you all made time to get to know your neighbors.

Speaker: W:
Text: Yes, but things have changed a lot.

Speaker: D:
Text: But you felt like this was your home?

Speaker: D:
Text: Since you’ve come here?

Speaker: W:
Text: Yes, I like that

Speaker: W:
Text: it’s nice and quiet.

Speaker: D:
Text: What kind of things would you all do for fun here in Crescent City?

Speaker: W:
Text: What kind?

Speaker: D:
Text: Uh-huh, you all go to a river, would you go to St. Augustine, or?

Speaker: W:
Text: I drove to the lake, and drive down to the lake, go back to the thrift stores, and go to the stores in the community and talked with the people, and I enjoyed that.

Speaker: D:
Text: Okay.

Speaker: D:
Text: Are you a part of any community organizations?

Speaker: W:
Text: Not really, unh-uh.

Speaker: D:
Text: So the church that you go to, was that the initial church, your first church you came to when you came to Crescent City?

Speaker: W:
Text: No, I used to go to Our Jethro.

Speaker: D:
Text: Okay.

Speaker: W:
Text: Went up there a couple of times.

Speaker: D:
Text: You continue to go?

Speaker: W:
Text: And then I found the other church, House of God, and I loved that better than the one, than Jethro.

Speaker: W:
Text: So that’s the one I go in, and that’s where I’ve been.

Speaker: W:
Text: And I love being there, love my church.

Speaker: D:
Text: So when would you go back and visit home?

Speaker: D:
Text: And visit Hastings?

Speaker: D:
Text: How often?

Speaker: W:
Text: Probably maybe in the future or something like that.

Speaker: W:
Text: When I have more time.

Speaker: W:
Text: Because I enjoy working in my community, and helping people.

Speaker: W:
Text: That’s what I do most here.

Speaker: D:
Text: You have any funny stories from Hastings?

Speaker: W:
Text: Just memories, a lot of memories with mom and dad, and my sisters, and our family gatherings, and we just have a good time.

Speaker: W:
Text: Something about the old time, old days, and everything, and we grew up and all, with all we did.

Speaker: W:
Text: Now mom and dad, and our grandparents.

Speaker: D:
Text: You felt like you learned a lot.

Speaker: W:
Text: Yes, they taught you a lot back then.

Speaker: D:
Text: What was one thing that stuck with you?

Speaker: W:
Text: Being raised up and spending time with my grandparents.

Speaker: D:
Text: So spending time with family?

Speaker: W:
Text: Uh-huh, and with family, I enjoyed that.

Speaker: D:
Text: What did your granddad do?

Speaker: W:
Text: He was a farm worker, worked on the farm.

Speaker: D:
Text: What was his name?

Speaker: W:
Text: His name was Emery Dean.

Speaker: D:
Text: Were they from Georgia too?

Speaker: W:
Text: Yes, my grandparents.

Speaker: W:
Text: They was all from Georgia.

Speaker: D:
Text: And those were the grandparents on your mom’s side?

Speaker: W:
Text: Uh-huh.

Speaker: D:
Text: Did you know grandparents on your dad’s side?

Speaker: W:
Text: Yes, my grandmother, she was from Georgia on my dad’s side.

Speaker: D:
Text: What was her name?

Speaker: W:
Text: Her name was Beulah Cobbs.

Speaker: D:
Text: Okay.

Speaker: D:
Text: Did he talk about his dad?

Speaker: W:
Text: Not too much about his dad.

Speaker: W:
Text: He always talked about his mom.

Speaker: D:
Text: Did you get to meet her?

Speaker: W:
Text: Yes, uh-

Speaker: W:
Text: huh.

Speaker: W:
Text: Used to go visit her in Georgia.

Speaker: D:
Text: What was the trip like?

Speaker: W:
Text: Hm?

Speaker: D:
Text: What was the trip like?

Speaker: W:
Text: It was nice.

Speaker: D:
Text: How’d you travel?

Speaker: W:
Text: In my dad’s car.

Speaker: D:
Text: What kind of things would she have for you all when you got there?

Speaker: W:
Text: She would have food cooked, and cakes baked.

Speaker: W:
Text: Nice.

Speaker: D:
Text: What would you go when you go there?

Speaker: W:
Text: We would just talk and play among ourselves.

Speaker: W:
Text: Just really enjoy seeing her.

Speaker: D:
Text: You got to travel a little bit growing up?

Speaker: W:
Text: Yes.

Speaker: D:
Text: Where are some other places you went to?

Speaker: W:
Text: Oh we did migrant work.

Speaker: W:
Text: We went to Dela — what it was, Virginia, and Delaware and we gathered crops during the summer.

Speaker: W:
Text: Yeah, worked in the fields.

Speaker: W:
Text: Picking tomatoes, and beans, and potatoes.

Speaker: D:
Text: So you all were on the road for a little while?

Speaker: W:
Text: Yes, we would travel.

Speaker: D:
Text: Throughout the year?

Speaker: W:
Text: Uh-huh.

Speaker: D:
Text: Did you like that?

Speaker: D:
Text: Or did you like being home?

Speaker: W:
Text: I prefer being home, but we had to leave and go with our parents to do what our parents told us to do.

Speaker: W:
Text: We had to obey.

Speaker: D:
Text: But you wanted to do something else.

Speaker: W:
Text: They wanted to go up there, they want you to leave home.

Speaker: W:
Text: You want to just stay home.

Speaker: D:
Text: So that’s how you all made money?

Speaker: W:
Text: Yes, we went and worked and made money to pay our bills and buy our school clothes.

Speaker: D:
Text: Who took care of the house while y’all were away?

Speaker: W:
Text: It was just there.

Speaker: W:
Text: Stayed there till we came back.

Speaker: W:
Text: It’ll be a house alone.

Speaker: D:
Text: No animals, or?

Speaker: W:
Text: No, we didn’t have any.

Speaker: D:
Text: Okay.

Speaker: D:
Text: Are there any other things you wanna add?

Speaker: W:
Text: Not really.

Speaker: D:
Text: Any you could think of?

Speaker: D:
Text: No, I just enjoyed raising my children, and getting them grown, so they can go their own separate ways.

Speaker: D:
Text: I enjoyed raising them, and talking to them, and trying to instill things of value into them, so that when they gotten grown, they already know how to take care of themselves and how to provide for themselves, and take care of themselves.

Speaker: D:
Text: Because that’s very important.

Speaker: D:
Text: Your sons more than your daughters, do you feel like they felt they faced more challenges being Black men, or was it hard for Black men and women, period?

Speaker: W:
Text: It was just hard for all.

Speaker: W:
Text: The mens and the womens.

Speaker: D:
Text: So you prepared them.

Speaker: D:
Text: Well, we can always schedule another interview, talk about other things.

Speaker: D:
Text: But thank you for your time.

Speaker: D:
Text: For letting m e get some history of you, of Hastings, and Crescent City.

Speaker: W:
Text: Thank you.

Text: So what do you do now?

Speaker: W:
Text: Hm?

Speaker: D:
Text: So what do you do now?

Speaker: W:
Text: What do I do now?

Speaker: D:
Text: Uh-huh.

Speaker: W:
Text: Well, if I’m home in my house.

Speaker: D:
Text: Yeah, I mean you were — done a lot of different jobs.

Speaker: D:
Text: Mom, field worker, so what do you do now?

Speaker: W:
Text: Mostly like retired at this moment and just helping the community, that’s what I do now.

Speaker: W:
Text: And my feet being burned is — I’m aggravated.

Speaker: W:
Text: I can’t get up and get out and do like how I used to do.

Speaker: W:
Text: See about the people in the community.

Speaker: W:
Text: I enjoy, that’s my happiness, because I love people.

Speaker: W:
Text: I can’t get up and get out like I used to, and drive my car, and go do things for people.

Speaker: D:
Text: Yeah, but you’ve been pretty healthy your whole life right?

Speaker: W:
Text: Yes.

Speaker: D:
Text: When you first were starting to go to the doctor, did you have a Black physician, or White, or did you have a choice?

Speaker: W:
Text: I had different ones.

Speaker: D:
Text: Okay.

Speaker: W:
Text: Both races.

Speaker: W:
Text: Black, White.

Text: Do you feel like medicine has advanced, has made some progress compared to?

Speaker: W:
Text: Yes, it has.

Speaker: D:
Text: Treatment?

Speaker: W:
Text: Right.

Text: Did you work in the health field before?

Speaker: W:
Text: No.
